title: Kenya has made significant progress under Ruto's leadership - Kindiki
summary: Deputy President Kithure Kindiki chairs a meeting with NLC Chairperson, Commissioners and Chief Executive Officer in Karen, Nairobi on July 14, 2026. Photo/DPCSDeputy President Kithure Kindiki has said Kenya has made significant progress in economic empowerment, healthcare, education and infrastructure under President William Ruto’s leadership.Speaking during Mashujaa Day celebrations at Kipchoge Keino Stadium in Eldoret, Uasin Gishu County, Kindiki said the country had made strides in improving the livelihoods of Kenyans over the past four years.He cited government interventions targeting farmers, expanded health coverage and efforts to strengthen social and economic rights as some of the achievements made under the current administration.Kindiki said Kenya had also made progress in governance, democracy and civil liberties in the 63 years since gaining independence.“During that journey, we have struggled with the project Kenya. We have struggled to continually improve the quality of life in our nation,” he said.The Deputy President said the country’s remaining task was to build on the accomplishments made since independence, with a focus on economic empowerment.He described the last four years under Ruto’s administration as defining for the country, pointing to efforts to improve access to essential services and strengthen the agricultural sector.“Under your leadership, a lot of progress has been made to improve livelihood and empower farmers. Cheaper fertilizers, cheaper seeds, cheaper artificial insemination for our dairy farmers,” Kindiki said.He added that the government had made progress in improving productivity in the coffee, tea and sugarcane sectors, as well as supporting fishing communities and people who depend on the blue economy.On healthcare, Kindiki said the government had increased the number of Kenyans covered under the Social Health Authority (SHA).He also cited progress in education and infrastructure development, saying the achievements should provide a foundation for further transformation.Kindiki urged the country to maintain momentum in the coming years, saying the next phase of development should deliver lasting improvements to the lives of Kenyans.“Today, we are here to listen to you, Your Excellency, as you speak to our nation to inspire us, so this final push will not only be defining but also permanently transform our country for good into the future,” he said.The Deputy President also expressed gratitude for serving alongside Ruto, pledging to continue supporting the administration’s development agenda. ©Citizen Digital, Kenya

title: Ethiopian Prime Minister calls for stronger trade ties with Kenya

We build as partners. In Ethiopia, we call this spirit Madama. It means synergy,” Abiy said.“Since 2022, it has carried clean power across our border. It brings light to homes and energy to industry. We also see it on the road from Mombasa to Hawassa. Our partnership grows through our businesses,” Abiya added.He said Safaricom has played a major role in promoting business, enabling Ethiopia and Kenya to trade more easily.“Today, Safaricom connects millions of Ethiopians and Mpesa helps people send money and make payments,” Abiya said.Abiya urged President William Ruto to continue with the partnership that will grow mainly through business. “Our farmers and producers must be able to trade more easily across our borders. Let more of our people visit each other's countries, discover our cultures, and learn together."The Ethiopian Prime Minister told President Ruto their partnership would benefit more families through business.He affirmed to the people of Kenya that Ethiopia will always support them. ©Citizen Digital, Kenya

title: Japan probe on its way to Mars moon
summary: People watch the launch of the H3 rocket, carrying the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft, at the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture on October 20, 2026.A Japanese spacecraft was on its way to one of Mars's moons on Tuesday on a world-first mission to retrieve samples, potentially helping unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth.The flagship H3 rocket carrying the unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe blasted off into a pitch black sky from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41 am (1941 GMT Monday), according to a live stream broadcast by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency.Over an hour later, JAXA announced via the live broadcast that the probe had successfully separated from the H3 and was "beginning its journey toward the Martian system"."I'd dreamt of this day, so I'm incredibly happy," said JAXA scientist Mari Aida. "Right now I feel really relieved."Following the separation, JAXA said it received signals from the spacecraft as expected, confirming it was operating normally.Despite the early hour in Japan, thousands of people tuned into the live stream, posting messages of encouragement.The spacecraft is due to arrive near Mars around August next year, where it will orbit one of its moons, Phobos.A French-German rover dubbed IDEFIX -- the French name for the comic hero Asterix's dog -- will be the first vehicle to travel across Phobos, conducting surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing.Once MMX arrives on Phobos, it will collect at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material from the surface during its planned three years in the Red Planet's vicinity.The mission -- which aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region -- is a collaboration with US and European space agencies, as well as numerous universities and tech companies.- 'Paradigm-shifting science'-Scientists hope it will help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration."The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars," Nicky Fox, administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a message broadcast on the JAXA live stream.JAXA hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born.One theory for the origin of the moons -- the "giant impact" hypothesis -- is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars.The "capture" hypothesis, meanwhile, postulates that the moons are asteroids pulled in by Mars's gravity.Determining which theory is correct will help reveal "how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets", JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun -- Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.JAXA said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a "natural space station" by establishing the requirements for a round trip -- something "essential for crewed Mars exploration".It will also observe the planet's other moon, Deimos, although it will not land on it.US and Chinese space agencies have also been vying to be the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars back to Earth.NASA's Perseverance rover, which has been roaming across Mars since 2021, has already collected samples.The return mission, however, was effectively cancelled by the administration of President Donald Trump following a vote by Congress in January.China's Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 -- potentially before the Japanese mission's return. ©Citizen Digital, Kenya
